claims.evidence: The extension of corticospinal distribution is observed in anatomical labeling shown in Figures 1B-D.

claims.claim: Corticospinal labeling was weaker or absent within the hindlimb S1 region itself.
claims.source: Corticospinal labeling was weaker or absent within the hindlimb S1 region itself, and also within the lateral part of the hand subfield corresponding to the D1/thenar subregion.
claims.evidence: The absence or weakness of corticospinal labeling in specific regions is observed in anatomical data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claims.claim: Corticospinal labeling was weaker or absent within the lateral part of the hand subfield corresponding to the D1/thenar subregion.
claims.source: Corticospinal labeling was weaker or absent within the hindlimb S1 region itself, and also within the lateral part of the hand subfield corresponding to the D1/thenar subregion.
claims.evidence: The absence or weakness of corticospinal labeling in the D1/thenar region is observed in anatomical data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claims.claim: The horizontal distribution of corticospinal neurons extends from M1 into S1, up to ~0.3 mm laterally below the labeled L4 of hand S1.
claims.source: Images of coronal sections gave similar results, confirming that the horizontal distribution of corticospinal neurons, which are located in L5B, extends from M1 into S1, up to ~0.3 mm laterally below the labeled L4 of hand S1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
claims.evidence: The extent of corticospinal neuron distribution is measured from coronal sections shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: Corticospinal labeling was observed in the region commonly identified as forelimb M1, medial to the L4 territory defining S1.
claims.source: Corticospinal labeling was observed in the region commonly identified as forelimb M1, medial to the L4 territory defining S1 (Ayling et al., 2009; Tennant et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The location of corticospinal labeling is observed in transcranial imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G) and compared to prior studies (Ayling et al., 2009; Tennant et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The distribution of cervically projecting corticospinal neurons extends toward and partially into the medial subregion of hand S1.
claims.source: However, as noted previously (Ueno et al., 2018), the distribution of cervically projecting corticospinal neurons also appeared to extend toward and partially into the medial subregion of hand S1.
claims.evidence: The extension of corticospinal neurons into S1 is observed in transcranial imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G) and is consistent with prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Responses to tactile stimulation of the fifth digit (D5) were located in a region corresponding to the posteromedial part of hand S1, in the region of overlap with corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: Then, for higher resolution imaging restricted to S1 areas, we used Scnn1a-Cre;GCaMP6s mice to label L4 neurons in S1 areas, which showed that responses to tactile stimulation of the fifth digit (D5) were located in a region corresponding to the posteromedial part of hand S1, in the region of overlap with corticospinal neurons, with the D2 representation located more anterior and lateral (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: The location of D5 responses is determined by functional imaging shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The D2 representation is located more anterior and lateral compared to the D5 representation in hand S1.
claims.source: Then, for higher resolution imaging restricted to S1 areas, we used Scnn1a-Cre;GCaMP6s mice to label L4 neurons in S1 areas, which showed that responses to tactile stimulation of the fifth digit (D5) were located in a region corresponding to the posteromedial part of hand S1, in the region of overlap with corticospinal neurons, with the D2 representation located more anterior and lateral (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: The location of D2 responses relative to D5 is determined by functional imaging shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The region of partial overlap between corticospinal neurons and hand S1 occurs in a medial part of S1 corresponding to the hypothenar/ulnar subregion of the somatotopic representation of the hand/forelimb area.
claims.source: These results, which build on and extend recent characterizations of hand/forelimb-related region of mouse S1 as it relates to the areal distribution of corticospinalC6-proj neurons (Ueno et al., 2018), demonstrate that the region of partial overlap occurs in a medial part of S1 corresponding to the hypothenar/ulnar subregion of the somatotopic representation of the hand/forelimb area.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the anatomical and functional mapping data presented in Figure 1 and builds on prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

claims.claim: After 72 hr incubation, PRV-Introvert-GFP injected into hand S1 of Scnn1a-Cre mice produced Cre-dependent labeling primarily at the injection site in S1, largely restricted to L4 neurons, with additional labeling in a small subregion of the VPL nucleus.
claims.source: After 72 hr (n = 3 mice), Cre-dependent labeling was observed primarily at the injection site in S1, largely restricted to L4 neurons, with additional labeling in a small subregion of the VPL nucleus (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The labeling pattern is directly observed in PRV tracing experiments shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: After 96 hr incubation, PRV-Introvert-GFP labeling was stronger at the S1 injection site and VPL, and also appeared in the cuneate nucleus.
claims.source: After longer incubation periods (96 hr; n = 3 mice), labeling was stronger at these sites, and also appeared in the cuneate nucleus (Figure 2C,D).
claims.evidence: The labeling pattern at 96 hr is directly observed in PRV tracing experiments shown in Figure 2C,D.

claims.claim: The timing of PRV spread to the cuneate suggests a disynaptic lemnisco-cortical circuit (cuneate→VPL→S1-L4).
claims.source: Nevertheless, the timing of the spread to the cuneate suggests a disynaptic lemnisco-cortical circuit (i.e., cuneate→VPL→S1-L4).
claims.evidence: The disynaptic nature is inferred from the temporal progression of PRV labeling from S1 to VPL (72 hr) to cuneate (96 hr).

claims.claim: Injection of retrograde tracer into VPL labeled the cuneate nucleus.
claims.source: Consistent with the PRV results, injection of retrograde tracer into VPL labeled the cuneate nucleus (n = 3 mice) (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: The labeling is directly observed in retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 3A–C.

claims.claim: Injection of retrograde tracer into PO did not label the cuneate but did label the trigeminal nucleus.
claims.source: Injection into PO in the same animals did not label the cuneate but did label the trigeminal nucleus (Figure 3D), likely due to spread of tracer into the whisker-related subregion of PO receiving paralemniscal afferents.
claims.evidence: The labeling pattern is directly observed in retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Following injection of anterograde tracer into the cuneate and retrograde tracer into S1, anatomical overlap of cuneate axons and somata of S1-projecting neurons was observed in VPL in a restricted region.
claims.source: Similarly, following injection of anterograde tracer into the cuneate and retrograde tracer into S1, in thalamic sections we observed anatomical overlap of cuneate axons and somata of S1-projecting neurons in VPL in a restricted region (n = 6 mice) (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: The overlap is directly observed in combined anterograde and retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 3E,F.

claims.claim: Cuneate axons were not observed in other thalamic nuclei (e.g. PO, VL).
claims.source: Cuneate axons were not observed in other thalamic nuclei (e.g. PO, VL), confirming in the mouse that the main ascending cuneothalamic projection is the medial lemniscal pathway to the VPL.
claims.evidence: The absence of cuneate axons in other thalamic nuclei is observed in anterograde tracing experiments and confirms the specificity of the cuneate→VPL pathway.

claims.claim: The main ascending cuneothalamic projection in the mouse is the medial lemniscal pathway to the VPL.
claims.source: Cuneate axons were not observed in other thalamic nuclei (e.g. PO, VL), confirming in the mouse that the main ascending cuneothalamic projection is the medial lemniscal pathway to the VPL.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the observation that cuneate axons are found only in VPL and not in other thalamic nuclei.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of ChR2-expressing cuneothalamic axons generated excitatory responses in VPL neurons that were strong (amplitude −158 ± 64 pA).
claims.source: These recordings showed excitatory responses that, although detected in only ~50% of the sampled neurons (n = 11 neurons, out of 23 neurons tested, with response amplitudes more than three times the baseline s.d.), tended to be strong (amplitude −158 ± 64 pA, mean ± s.e.m.) (Figure 3G,H).
claims.evidence: The response amplitude is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 3G,H.

claims.claim: Cuneothalamic excitatory responses in VPL neurons were blocked by NMDA and AMPA receptor antagonists.
claims.source: These inputs were blocked by NMDA and AMPA receptor antagonists (1 µM CPP, 10 µM NBQX, n = 3 neurons) and showed short-term depression upon repetitive stimulation (2nd/1st response amplitude: 0.62 ± 0.04; n = 7 neurons, mean ± s.e.m.; p=0.016, sign test) (Figure 3H,I).
claims.evidence: The pharmacological blockade is demonstrated experimentally in recordings shown in Figure 3H,I.

claims.claim: Cuneothalamic excitatory responses in VPL neurons showed short-term depression upon repetitive stimulation (2nd/1st response amplitude: 0.62 ± 0.04).
claims.source: These inputs were blocked by NMDA and AMPA receptor antagonists (1 µM CPP, 10 µM NBQX, n = 3 neurons) and showed short-term depression upon repetitive stimulation (2nd/1st response amplitude: 0.62 ± 0.04; n = 7 neurons, mean ± s.e.m.; p=0.016, sign test) (Figure 3H,I).
claims.evidence: Short-term depression is measured from repetitive stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3H,I.

claims.claim: Cuneothalamic inputs to VPL neurons accord with prior results for lemniscal-type inputs to VPM neurons in whisker-related circuits.
claims.source: These findings accord with prior results for lemniscal-type inputs to VPM neurons in the whisker-related circuits (Mo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The comparison is made to prior work on VPM inputs (Mo et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Injection of AAV-hSyn-Cre into the cuneate resulted in labeled neurons in the dorsal column nuclei.
claims.source: In WT mice, we injected AAV-hSyn-Cre into the cuneate and, to visualize the labeling of cuneate neurons, co-injected AAV-Flex-EGFP, resulting in labeled neurons in the dorsal column nuclei (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The labeling is directly observed in viral tracing experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Injection of Cre-dependent AAV-ChR2 into VPL of mice with AAV-hSyn-Cre in cuneate resulted in labeling of cuneo-recipient VPL neurons.
claims.source: We additionally injected the VPL, the target of the cuneothalamic projection, with a Cre-dependent AAV-ChR2. This resulted in labeling of CuN-recVPL neurons (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The labeling of cuneo-recipient VPL neurons is directly observed in viral tracing experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Labeled axons from cuneo-recipient VPL neurons were observed in L4 of S1.
claims.source: In S1 slices, labeled axons from the CuN-recVPL neurons were seen in L4, along with retrogradely labeled corticocortical L2/3M1-proj and L5AM1-proj neurons, and corticospinalC6-proj neurons in L5B (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The axonal labeling in L4 is directly observed in anatomical sections shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Cuneo-recipient VPL input to S1 was strongest to L4 neurons, with weaker input to corticocortical M1-projecting neurons in L2/3 and L5A, and little or no direct excitation of corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: We observed a pattern of strongest input to L4 neurons, moderate-to-low input to L2/3M1-proj and L5AM1-proj neurons, and little or no input to corticospinalC6-proj neurons (n = 9 quadruplets, four mice; p=0.00001, Kruskal-Wallis test) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: VPL axons ramified most densely in L4 of S1.
claims.source: Images of the cortical labeling pattern showed, as expected based on the labeling studies described earlier, that the anterogradely labeled VPL axons ramified most densely in L4 of S1, with corticospinalC6-proj neuron distributions found in forelimb M1 with extension into S1 as well, below the barrel-like clusters of VPL axons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The axonal ramification pattern is directly observed in anatomical labeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Responses to photostimulation of VPL axons were strongest in L4 neurons, and weaker in corticocortical M1-projecting neurons.
claims.source: Electrophysiological recordings in coronal S1 slices showed that responses to photostimulation of VPL axons were strongest in L4 neurons, and weaker in corticocorticalM1-proj (n = 15, 10, and eight for L2/3M1-proj, L4, and L5AM1-proj neurons; eight mice; L2/3M1-proj vs L4, p=0.0004; L4 vs L5AM1-proj, p=0.00005; L2/3M1-proj vs L5AM1-proj, p=0.72; rank-sum test) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E.

claims.claim: VPL input to L4 neurons was strong, while input to corticospinal neurons was little or none.
claims.source: Additional recordings comparing the VPL input to L4 neurons and corticospinalC6-proj neurons showed strong input to the former, and little or no input to the latter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H) (n = 8 pairs, two mice; p=0.008, sign-test).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H.

claims.claim: Cuneo-recipient VPL neurons primarily target L4 neurons in hand S1, with weaker input to corticocortical M1-projecting neurons and little or no direct excitation of corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: These results thus provide a profile of CuN-recVPL input to hand S1, identifying L4 neurons as the primary targets, with weaker input to corticocorticalM1-proj neurons in the two adjacent layers and little or no direct excitation of corticospinalC6-proj neurons (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and summarized in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Strong L4→L2/3 connectivity exists in local circuits of forelimb S1 of the mouse.
claims.source: As previous work has shown strong L4→L2/3 connectivity in local circuits of forelimb S1 of the mouse (Yamawaki et al., 2014), the results indicate that those intracortical connections would augment the more direct but lower-amplitude CuN-recVPL→L2/3M1-proj connections.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Yamawaki et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Anterogradely labeled PO axons ramified in L1 and L5A of hand S1.
claims.source: The anterogradely labeled PO axons ramified in L1 and L5A (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The axonal ramification pattern is directly observed in anatomical labeling shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: PO inputs were strongest to L5A M1-projecting neurons, weak-to-moderate to L2/3 M1-projecting neurons, and mostly absent to L4 neurons in hand S1.
claims.source: PO inputs were strongest to L5M1-proj neurons, weak-to-moderate to L2/3M1-proj neurons, and mostly absent to L4 neurons (n = 9, 8, and 9 for L2/3M1-proj, L4, and L5AM1-proj neurons, respectively; 3 mice; L2/3M1-proj vs L4, p=0.022; L4 vs L5AM1-proj, p=0.00004; L2/3M1-proj vs L5AM1-proj, p=0.00004; rank-sum test) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: PO inputs to L5A neurons were stronger compared to corticospinal neurons in S1.
claims.source: Additional experiments showed stronger inputs to L5A neurons compared to other types of S1 projection neurons, including corticospinalC6-proj neurons (n = 9 L5A and 10 corticospinal neurons; 3 mice; p=0.004, sign-test) (Figure 5D)
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: PO inputs to L5A neurons were stronger compared to L5B PO-projecting neurons in S1.
claims.source: Additional experiments showed stronger inputs to L5A neurons compared to other types of S1 projection neurons, including corticospinalC6-proj neurons (n = 9 L5A and 10 corticospinal neurons; 3 mice; p=0.004, sign-test) (Figure 5D); L5BPO-proj neurons (n = 9 pairs; 4 mice; p=0.004, sign-test) (Figure 5E)
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: PO inputs to L5A neurons were stronger compared to corticothalamic L6 PO-projecting neurons in S1.
claims.source: Additional experiments showed stronger inputs to L5A neurons compared to other types of S1 projection neurons, including corticospinalC6-proj neurons (n = 9 L5A and 10 corticospinal neurons; 3 mice; p=0.004, sign-test) (Figure 5D); L5BPO-proj neurons (n = 9 pairs; 4 mice; p=0.004, sign-test) (Figure 5E); and, corticothalamic L6PO-proj neurons (n = 6 pairs; 2 mice; p=0.031, sign-test) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The main targets of PO projections to hand S1 are L5A neurons, including those forming corticocortical projections to forelimb M1.
claims.source: Thus, collectively these findings (Figure 5G) indicate that the main targets of PO projections to hand S1 are L5A neurons, including those forming corticocortical projections to forelimb M1, with additional input to M1-projecting neurons in L2/3 but notably weak or absent input to corticospinal and other major classes of neurons.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5C-F and summarized in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Retrograde labeling from M1 demonstrated labeling in S1 mainly of L2/3 and L5A neurons.
claims.source: Retrograde labeling from M1 demonstrated labeling in S1 mainly of L2/3 and L5A neurons (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The labeling pattern is directly observed in retrograde tracing shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Responses to photostimulation of S1 L5A/Tlx3 axons in M1 were strongest in L2/3 neurons, and generally either very weak or absent in pyramidal neurons in L5A, L6, and corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: Recordings in M1 slices showed that responses to photostimulation of S1 L5A/Tlx3 axons were strongest in L2/3 neurons, and generally either very weak or absent in pyramidal neurons in L5A and L6, and also in corticospinalC6-proj neurons (n = 12, 8, 9, and six for L2/3, L5A, corticospinalC6-proj, and L6 neurons, respectively, recorded as sets of neurons always including L2/3 neurons plus multiple other types; five mice; p=0.00001, Kruskal-Wallis test) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The L5A-originating component of the S1→M1 corticocortical circuit selectively excites postsynaptic L2/3 neurons.
claims.source: Thus, the L5A-originating component of the S1→M1 corticocortical circuit selectively excites postsynaptic L2/3 neurons (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6C and summarized in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: S1 corticocortical axons from shallow injections (mainly L2/3) primarily excited L2/3 neurons in forelimb M1, with weaker input to L5A neurons and weak or absent input to L5B neurons, including corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: Again the S1 corticocortical axons primarily excited L2/3 neurons in forelimb M1, with weaker input to L5A neurons and weak or absent input to L5B neurons, including corticospinal neurons (n = 6, 7, 5, 4, and six for L2/3, L5A, unlabeled L5B, corticospinalC6-proj, and L6 neurons, respectively, recorded as sets of neurons always including L2/3 neurons plus multiple other types; five mice; p=0.0004, Kruskal-Wallis test; corticospinalC6-proj is grouped with unlabeled L5B neurons) (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: The connectivity pattern is measured from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The L2/3-originating component of the S1→M1 corticocortical circuit selectively excites postsynaptic L2/3 neurons.
claims.source: Thus, the L2/3-originating component of the S1→M1 corticocortical circuit selectively also excites postsynaptic L2/3 neurons (Figure 6H), converging with the L5A-originating component.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6G and summarized in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: The main recipients of S1 corticocortical input to M1 are L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: These results add key details about the excitatory connectivity in the last stage along the transcortical circuit leading to M1, showing that the main recipients of S1 corticocortical input are L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6C and 6G.

claims.claim: L4 neurons in hand S1 strongly excite L2/3 neurons.
claims.source: In addition to the current findings, prior results show that the L4 neurons in hand S1 strongly excite L2/3 neurons (Yamawaki et al., 2014), and the L2/3 neurons in forelimb M1 strongly excite cervically projecting corticospinal neurons (Anderson et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Yamawaki et al., 2014).

claims.claim: L2/3 neurons in forelimb M1 strongly excite cervically projecting corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: In addition to the current findings, prior results show that the L4 neurons in hand S1 strongly excite L2/3 neurons (Yamawaki et al., 2014), and the L2/3 neurons in forelimb M1 strongly excite cervically projecting corticospinal neurons (Anderson et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Anderson et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Local L2/3 neurons in M1 are the critical penultimate excitatory link in the transcortical circuit, postsynaptic to S1 corticocortical axons and presynaptic to M1 corticospinal neurons.
claims.source: Thus, the present findings, together with prior circuit-mapping results, imply that local L2/3 neurons in M1 are the critical penultimate excitatory link in this transcortical circuit, postsynaptic to S1 corticocortical axons and presynaptic to M1 corticospinal neurons (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn by integrating the current findings with prior work (Yamawaki et al., 2014; Anderson et al., 2010) and summarized in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The lemnisco-cortical leg of the transcortical circuit has a 'streamlined' organization, spanning ~1 cm from cuneate to cortex via a single excitatory synapse in thalamus.
claims.source: A salient feature is the sharp contrast between the 'streamlined' organization of the lemnisco-cortical leg of the circuit, spanning the relatively large ~1 cm distance from cuneate to cortex via a single excitatory synapse in thalamus, and the densely polysynaptic organization of the corticocortical leg of the circuit, linking S1 to M1 across a mere ~1 mm distance but through complex circuits that engage multiple subtypes of intratelencephalic (IT) neurons (in L2 through L5A in S1, and in L2/3 in M1) en route to the M1 corticospinal neurons that close the transcortical loop by feeding into spinal circuits controlling motor neurons innervating forelimb muscles.
claims.evidence: The characterization is drawn from the overall circuit architecture revealed by the study's findings.

claims.claim: The corticocortical leg of the transcortical circuit has a densely polysynaptic organization, linking S1 to M1 across ~1 mm through complex circuits engaging multiple subtypes of intratelencephalic neurons.
claims.source: A salient feature is the sharp contrast between the 'streamlined' organization of the lemnisco-cortical leg of the circuit, spanning the relatively large ~1 cm distance from cuneate to cortex via a single excitatory synapse in thalamus, and the densely polysynaptic organization of the corticocortical leg of the circuit, linking S1 to M1 across a mere ~1 mm distance but through complex circuits that engage multiple subtypes of intratelencephalic (IT) neurons (in L2 through L5A in S1, and in L2/3 in M1) en route to the M1 corticospinal neurons that close the transcortical loop by feeding into spinal circuits controlling motor neurons innervating forelimb muscles.
claims.evidence: The characterization is drawn from the overall circuit architecture revealed by the study's findings.

claims.claim: The overall thalamocortical-corticocortical circuit architecture for hand-related pathways closely resembles the corresponding whisker-related S1→M1 circuits.
claims.source: The overall thalamocortical-corticocortical circuit architecture in many ways closely resembles the corresponding whisker-related S1→M1 circuits, which have mostly been studied piece-wise but also involve the concatenation of excitatory connections.
claims.evidence: The comparison is made based on the current findings and prior work on whisker-related circuits cited throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: One apparent difference in hand-related circuits compared to whisker-related circuits is that VPL inputs are notably weak to corticospinal neurons, whereas VPM inputs to L5B neurons in whisker S1 appear relatively stronger.
claims.source: One apparent difference in the hand-related circuits (in addition to the apparent lack of an ascending paralemniscal pathway to PO, discussed above) is that VPL inputs are notably weak to corticospinal neurons, representing a major subtype of pyramidal-tract type neurons in L5B, whereas VPM inputs to L5B neurons in whisker S1 appear relatively stronger and are implicated in early cortical processing of somatosensory signals (Petreanu et al., 2009; Wimmer et al., 2010; Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; Rah et al., 2013; Sermet et al., 2019; Egger et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The comparison is made based on the current findings and prior work on whisker-related circuits (Petreanu et al., 2009; Wimmer et al., 2010; Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; Rah et al., 2013; Sermet et al., 2019; Egger et al., 2020).

claims.claim: Corticospinal neurons in S1 in the overlap zone project to more dorsal levels of the spinal cord where they innervate distinct classes of spinal interneurons and are involved in more sensory-related aspects of forelimb motor behavior.
claims.source: Recent evidence reveals that corticospinal neurons in S1 in the overlap zone project to more dorsal levels of the spinal cord where they innervate distinct classes of spinal interneurons and are involved in more sensory-related aspects of forelimb motor behavior, whereas M1 corticospinal neurons project to more ventral cord levels and connect to spinal interneurons that directly contact spinal motor neurons (Ueno et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

claims.claim: M1 corticospinal neurons project to more ventral cord levels and connect to spinal interneurons that directly contact spinal motor neurons.
claims.source: Recent evidence reveals that corticospinal neurons in S1 in the overlap zone project to more dorsal levels of the spinal cord where they innervate distinct classes of spinal interneurons and are involved in more sensory-related aspects of forelimb motor behavior, whereas M1 corticospinal neurons project to more ventral cord levels and connect to spinal interneurons that directly contact spinal motor neurons (Ueno et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Forelimb S1 and M1 in the mouse are adjacent cortical areas, resembling the typical side-by-side topographic layout of somatosensory and motor areas seen in primates.
claims.source: This topography of the forelimb-related S1, adjacent to M1 and sharing the cortical distribution of corticospinal neurons, contrasts with that of the whisker-related areas in mouse cortex, where vibrissal S1 and M1 are widely separated as non-adjacent cortical areas. In this sense, forelimb S1 and M1 in the mouse resembles more the typical side-by-side topographic layout of somatosensory and motor areas seen in primates.
claims.evidence: The comparison is made based on the anatomical observations in the current study and general knowledge of primate cortical organization.

claims.claim: Vibrissal S1 and M1 in mouse cortex are widely separated as non-adjacent cortical areas.
claims.source: This topography of the forelimb-related S1, adjacent to M1 and sharing the cortical distribution of corticospinal neurons, contrasts with that of the whisker-related areas in mouse cortex, where vibrissal S1 and M1 are widely separated as non-adjacent cortical areas.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of mouse cortical anatomy.

claims.claim: The somatotopic layout of the forelimb subfield of mouse S1 shows relative expansion (cortical magnification) of the hand with respect to the rest of the forelimb.
claims.source: Another notable aspect of the somatotopic layout of the forelimb subfield of mouse S1 is the relative expansion, or cortical magnification, both of the hand with respect to the rest of the forelimb, and of the thumb/thenar representation with respect to the rest of the hand.
claims.evidence: The cortical magnification is observed in the anatomical data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The somatotopic layout of the forelimb subfield of mouse S1 shows relative expansion (cortical magnification) of the thumb/thenar representation with respect to the rest of the hand.
claims.source: Another notable aspect of the somatotopic layout of the forelimb subfield of mouse S1 is the relative expansion, or cortical magnification, both of the hand with respect to the rest of the forelimb, and of the thumb/thenar representation with respect to the rest of the hand.
claims.evidence: The cortical magnification is observed in the anatomical data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The cortical magnification pattern of hand and thumb representations has been observed in other mammalian species, ranging from rodents to primates and humans.
claims.source: This pattern has been observed in other mammalian species, ranging from other rodents such as rats and squirrels to other primates and humans (Sur et al., 1978; Waters et al., 1995; Jain et al., 2008; Krubitzer et al., 2011; Martuzzi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in various mammalian species.

claims.claim: Four days after injection of PRV-Introvert-GFP into hand S1 using the L5A-specific Tlx3-Cre mouse line, thalamic labeling was observed in PO but not in the cuneate nucleus.
claims.source: We attempted to identify a corresponding cuneo-PO paralemniscal pathway to hand S1 in the mouse by performing the same PRV experiment but with the L5A-specific Tlx3-Cre mouse line. However, 4 days (96 hr; n = 2 mice) after injection of PRV-Introvert-GFP into hand S1, we observed thalamic labeling in PO, but no cuneate labeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The labeling pattern is directly observed in PRV tracing experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Injection of PRV-EGFP into forelimb muscles (biceps) resulted in labeling of corticospinal neurons only in forelimb M1, not hand S1.
claims.source: As shown previously (Ueno et al., 2018), injection of PRV-EGFP into forelimb muscles (biceps) resulted in labeling (after 72 hr; n = 3 mice) of corticospinal neurons only in forelimb M1, not hand S1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The labeling pattern is directly observed in PRV tracing experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and is consistent with prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The feedforward thalamocortical circuits largely avoid direct innervation of thalamus-projecting neurons and instead engage mainly intratelencephalic type neurons.
claims.source: Thus, the available evidence suggests that the feedforward thalamocortical circuits largely avoid direct innervation of thalamus-projecting neurons and instead engage mainly intratelencephalic type neurons, including subtypes involved either mainly in local excitatory circuits (L4 neurons) or in both local and corticocortical circuits (L2/3, L5A neurons).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the connectivity patterns observed in the current study and prior work.

claims.claim: PO inputs show a strong bias toward L5A neurons, including L5A M1-projecting neurons, which appear as common elements shared by recurrent cortico-thalamo-cortical loops, local excitatory networks, and corticocortical circuits in the transcortical circuit.
claims.source: Particularly striking in this regard is the strong bias of PO inputs to L5A neurons, including L5AM1-proj neurons, which thus appear as common elements shared by recurrent cortico-thalamo-cortical loops, local excitatory networks, and corticocortical circuits in the transcortical circuit.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is drawn from the connectivity patterns observed in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The transcortical circuit can be conceptualized as an extended set of intersecting and selectively interconnecting looping circuits, within which the feedforward circuits are fully embedded.
claims.source: Another way to conceptualize this network is as an extended set of intersecting and selectively interconnecting looping circuits, within which the feedforward circuits constituting the transcortical circuit are fully embedded.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the circuit architecture revealed by the study's findings.

claims.claim: The patterns of excitatory connections for hand-related circuits generally resemble those known for vibrissal circuits, both for lemniscal VPM/VPL-related pathways and paralemniscal PO-related pathways.
claims.source: The overall picture to emerge is one of similarity. Both systems are, after all, part of the lemniscal pathway, the main ascending somatosensory system for tactile sensation: cuneo-VPL-cortical for the forelimb and trigemino-VPM-cortical for the vibrissae. The patterns of excitatory connections for the hand-related circuits (Figure 7) generally resemble those known for vibrissal circuits, both for the lemniscal VPM/VPL-related pathways and also the paralemniscal PO-related pathways (see references listed above; for recent reviews, see Adesnik and Naka, 2018; Staiger and Petersen, 2021; Shepherd and Yamawaki, 2021).
claims.evidence: The comparison is made based on the current findings and extensive prior work on whisker-related circuits cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: For the relatively short-distance corticocortical circuits, they adhere to the same pattern of targeting upper-layer neurons previously observed in the vibrissal S1-to-M1 projection.
claims.source: On the other hand, for the relatively short-distance corticocortical circuits studied here, it is striking that they adhere to the same pattern of targeting upper-layer neurons previously observed in the vibrissal S1-to-M1 projection, despite the greater distances bridged by the inter-areal projections in that pathway (Mao et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The comparison is made to prior work on whisker-related circuits (Mao et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The highly polysynaptic nature of the circuit organization at the cortical level suggests many possibilities for cellular mechanisms that may regulate and modulate the flow of excitation through the loop.
claims.source: The highly polysynaptic nature of the circuit organization at the cortical level suggests many possibilities for cellular mechanisms that may regulate and modulate the flow of excitation through the loop.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of the circuit architecture.

claims.claim: The dense incorporation of multiple types of IT neurons into the transcortical circuit may increase its computational power by providing an expanded array of targets by which local and long-range inputs from diverse sources can modulate excitatory feedforward signaling.
claims.source: Perhaps the dense incorporation of multiple types of IT neurons into this circuit increases its computational power by providing an expanded array of targets by which local and long-range inputs from diverse sources can modulate excitatory feedforward signaling along the connections feeding into M1 corticospinal neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional implications of the circuit architecture.

claims.claim: Mice display a variety of hand and forelimb movements including highly dexterous manipulation behaviors, directional reaching, and more.
claims.source: Mice offer a favorable model for investigating these hand-related transcortical circuits, as they display a variety of hand and forelimb movements including highly dexterous manipulation behaviors, directional reaching, and more (e.g. Whishaw et al., 1998; Guo et al., 2015; Galiñanes et al., 2018; Barrett et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies of mouse forelimb behavior.

claims.claim: Mice have a well-defined hand and forelimb representation in S1.
claims.source: Mice have a well-defined hand and forelimb representation in S1, and corticospinal neurons projecting to cells and circuits in the cervical spinal cord feeding into motor neurons innervating forelimb muscles (Ueno et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ueno et al., 2018) and the anatomical observations in the current study.

claims.claim: Mice have corticospinal neurons projecting to cells and circuits in the cervical spinal cord feeding into motor neurons innervating forelimb muscles.
claims.source: Mice have a well-defined hand and forelimb representation in S1, and corticospinal neurons projecting to cells and circuits in the cervical spinal cord feeding into motor neurons innervating forelimb muscles (Ueno et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The macroscopic structure of lemnisco-cortical and corticocortical pathways in the transcortical circuit is well-known from classical anatomy.
claims.source: The macroscopic structure of these lemnisco-cortical and corticocortical pathways is well-known from classical anatomy (Brodal, 1981) and supported by in vivo electrophysiology (Andersson, 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to classical anatomical work (Brodal, 1981) and electrophysiology (Andersson, 1995).

claims.claim: The cellular-level synaptic connectivity linking the major nodes of the transcortical pathway remains largely uncharacterized for hand-related circuits.
claims.source: However, the cellular-level synaptic connectivity linking the major nodes, whereby peripheral inputs are ultimately conveyed to corticospinal neurons in S1 and/or M1, remains largely uncharacterized for these hand-related circuits.
claims.evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: Much is known about the circuit connections and structure-function relationships in corresponding transcortical pathways in the whisker-barrel system of rats and mice.
claims.source: In contrast, much is known about the circuit connections and structure-function relationships in corresponding transcortical pathways in the whisker-barrel system of rats and mice (Feldmeyer, 2012; Feldmeyer et al., 2013; Petersen, 2019; Staiger and Petersen, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to reviews of whisker-barrel system circuits.

claims.claim: The whisker-barrel system includes lemniscal and corticocortical pathways traversing VPM, whisker S1, and whisker M1, as well as a paralemniscal pathway conveying whisking-related signals via PO.
claims.source: Similar to the hand-related pathways, the ascending somatosensory pathways in this system include lemniscal and corticocortical pathways traversing the ventral posterior medial (VPM) nucleus, whisker S1, and whisker M1; additionally, however, a paralemniscal pathway conveys whisking-related signals via the posterior (PO) nucleus.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of whisker-barrel system anatomy.

claims.claim: The whisker and hand/forelimb systems differ in fundamental ways, including the structure and function of the sensors, proprioceptive systems, and modes of operation.
claims.source: While both systems are used for active sensing, they differ in fundamental ways, ranging from the structure and function of the sensors (actively whisked vibrissal hairs versus glabrous pads and hairy skin) and proprioceptive systems (muscle spindles present in forelimb but largely absent in vibrissal musculature) (Moore et al., 2015; Severson et al., 2019) to the modes of operation (bilaterally coupled oscillatory whisking versus diverse forelimb movements for manipulation and locomotion).
claims.evidence: The differences are stated based on established knowledge and cited references (Moore et al., 2015; Severson et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The S1 and M1 areas for whiskers are widely separated, whereas those for the hand/forelimb are side-by-side.
claims.source: Differences in pathway anatomy may reflect these behavioral specializations; the S1 and M1 areas for the whiskers are widely separated, whereas those for the hand/forelimb are side-by-side, and the primary source of corticocortical input to whisker M1 is the contralateral whisker M1, whereas that for forelimb M1 is the adjacent ipsilateral forelimb S1, suggesting a more prominent role of somatosensory feedback (Colechio and Alloway, 2009).
claims.evidence: The anatomical difference is stated based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The primary source of corticocortical input to whisker M1 is the contralateral whisker M1, whereas that for forelimb M1 is the adjacent ipsilateral forelimb S1.
claims.source: Differences in pathway anatomy may reflect these behavioral specializations; the S1 and M1 areas for the whiskers are widely separated, whereas those for the hand/forelimb are side-by-side, and the primary source of corticocortical input to whisker M1 is the contralateral whisker M1, whereas that for forelimb M1 is the adjacent ipsilateral forelimb S1, suggesting a more prominent role of somatosensory feedback (Colechio and Alloway, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Colechio and Alloway, 2009).

claims.claim: The anatomical organization of forelimb M1 input suggests a more prominent role of somatosensory feedback compared to whisker M1.
claims.source: Differences in pathway anatomy may reflect these behavioral specializations; the S1 and M1 areas for the whiskers are widely separated, whereas those for the hand/forelimb are side-by-side, and the primary source of corticocortical input to whisker M1 is the contralateral whisker M1, whereas that for forelimb M1 is the adjacent ipsilateral forelimb S1, suggesting a more prominent role of somatosensory feedback (Colechio and Alloway, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical differences and cited work (Colechio and Alloway, 2009).

results.result: The hand/forelimb S1 subfield in mice contains barrel-like structures arranged in a somatotopic pattern similar to rats, with D1/thenar representation lateral and D5/hypothenar medial, separated by septa. This pattern represents a conserved mammalian organizational feature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 collectively establish the somatotopic organization of mouse hand S1 through direct anatomical observations (Figure 1A) and comparisons to well-established rat anatomy (Waters et al., 1995). The presence of barrel-like structures, their spatial arrangement, and septa are directly visualized. The conservation across mammals is supported by multiple citations to studies in various species.

results.result: Corticospinal neurons labeled by cervical C6 injection are distributed primarily in M1 but extend partially into the medial edge of hand S1, specifically the D5/hypothenar region, with weaker or absent labeling in hindlimb S1 and the lateral D1/thenar region.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C16 are supported by direct anatomical observations from retrograde labeling experiments (Figures 1B-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The spatial distribution, extent of overlap (~0.3 mm), and regional specificity are quantitatively documented. The findings are consistent with prior work (Ueno et al., 2018).

results.result: Functional mapping confirms that the region of overlap between corticospinal neurons and hand S1 corresponds to the hypothenar/ulnar subregion, with D5 responses located posteromedially and D2 responses more anterior and lateral.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by functional imaging data (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I) that directly map somatosensory responses to specific digits. The functional data corroborate the anatomical characterization and are consistent with prior work (Ueno et al., 2018). The integration of anatomical and functional evidence strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: PRV tracing from L4 neurons in hand S1 reveals a disynaptic lemnisco-cortical pathway: cuneate→VPL→S1-L4, with labeling appearing in VPL at 72 hr and cuneate at 96 hr post-injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by direct observations from PRV tracing experiments (Figure 2A-D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The temporal progression of labeling provides evidence for the disynaptic nature of the circuit. However, the authors acknowledge that precise timing may be influenced by multiple factors including Cre-mediated expression kinetics and variable starter cell numbers.

results.result: Retrograde and anterograde tracing confirms that the cuneate nucleus projects specifically to VPL (not PO or other thalamic nuclei), establishing the medial lemniscal pathway as the main ascending cuneothalamic projection in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by multiple complementary tracing experiments (Figure 3A-F). Retrograde tracing from VPL labels cuneate but not from PO; anterograde tracing from cuneate labels only VPL among thalamic nuclei. The convergence of evidence from different approaches strengthens the conclusion about pathway specificity.

results.result: Cuneothalamic synaptic connections to VPL neurons are strong (−158 ± 64 pA), glutamatergic (blocked by NMDA/AMPA antagonists), and show short-term depression (2nd/1st ratio: 0.62 ± 0.04), consistent with lemniscal-type driver inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by direct electrophysiological measurements (Figure 3G-I) with appropriate pharmacological controls and statistical testing (p=0.016, n=7). The properties match expectations for lemniscal inputs and are consistent with prior work on VPM (Mo et al., 2017). However, responses were detected in only ~50% of sampled neurons, likely due to fine-scale somatotopic organization.

results.result: Cuneo-recipient VPL neurons primarily target L4 neurons in hand S1, with weaker input to L2/3 and L5A M1-projecting neurons, and little or no direct excitation of corticospinal neurons, as demonstrated by a novel anterograde transneuronal labeling approach combined with electrophysiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C39 are supported by converging evidence from anatomical labeling (Figure 4B-D) and electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The novel AAV-hSyn-Cre transneuronal approach enables selective labeling of cuneo-recipient VPL neurons. Statistical testing confirms significant differences in connectivity strength (p=0.00001, Kruskal-Wallis test; n=9 quadruplets). Multiple complementary experiments strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Strong L4→L2/3 connectivity exists in local circuits of forelimb S1, which would augment the weaker direct VPL→L2/3 connections.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is supported by citation to prior work (Yamawaki et al., 2014) that directly demonstrated this connectivity. The authors appropriately integrate this established finding with their current results to interpret the functional implications of the circuit architecture.

results.result: PO inputs to hand S1 primarily target L5A neurons (including M1-projecting neurons), with weaker input to L2/3 and minimal input to L4, corticospinal, and other projection neuron types, representing a distinct connectivity pattern from VPL inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by anatomical observations (Figure 5B) and systematic electrophysiological comparisons across multiple neuron types (Figure 5C-F). Statistical testing confirms significant differences (p-values ranging from 0.00004 to 0.031, n=3-4 mice). The selective targeting of L5A neurons is consistently demonstrated across multiple comparisons.

results.result: S1→M1 corticocortical projections from both L5A and L2/3 neurons selectively target L2/3 pyramidal neurons in M1, with weak or absent input to L5A, L5B (including corticospinal), and L6 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by anatomical tracing (Figure 4D, 6B, 6F) and electrophysiological recordings from identified projection neurons (Figure 6C, 6G). Statistical testing confirms significant differences in connectivity (p=0.00001 and p=0.0004, Kruskal-Wallis tests; n=5 mice each). The convergence of L5A and L2/3 projections onto M1 L2/3 neurons is demonstrated by two independent experimental approaches.

results.result: Integration of current findings with prior work establishes that L2/3 neurons in M1 are the critical penultimate excitatory link in the transcortical circuit, receiving input from S1 L4→L2/3→M1 pathways and projecting to M1 corticospinal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 integrate the current findings with well-established prior results (Yamawaki et al., 2014; Anderson et al., 2010). The synthesis is logical and supported by the convergence of evidence from multiple studies. The conclusion about L2/3 neurons as the penultimate link is a reasonable inference from the combined data, though it represents an integration of findings rather than a direct demonstration in the current study.

results.result: The transcortical circuit exhibits contrasting organizational features: a 'streamlined' lemnisco-cortical leg spanning ~1 cm via a single thalamic synapse, versus a densely polysynaptic corticocortical leg spanning ~1 mm through multiple intratelencephalic neuron subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 represent a synthesis of the circuit architecture revealed by the study's findings. The characterization is supported by the anatomical and functional data presented throughout the manuscript. The contrast between the two circuit legs is a valid interpretation of the overall organization, though the specific distance measurements and synapse counts should be considered approximate.

results.result: Hand-related transcortical circuits closely resemble whisker-related circuits in overall architecture, with one notable difference being weaker VPL inputs to corticospinal neurons in hand circuits compared to relatively stronger VPM inputs to L5B neurons in whisker circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by systematic comparison of the current findings to extensive prior work on whisker circuits (multiple citations throughout). The similarity in overall architecture is well-documented. The difference in thalamic input strength to L5B neurons is supported by the current data and prior studies (Petreanu et al., 2009; Wimmer et al., 2010; Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; Rah et al., 2013; Sermet et al., 2019; Egger et al., 2020).

results.result: Corticospinal neurons in S1 and M1 have distinct spinal targets and functional roles: S1 corticospinal neurons project to dorsal spinal cord and are involved in sensory-related aspects of forelimb behavior, while M1 corticospinal neurons project to ventral cord and connect to motor neuron-contacting interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by citation to prior work (Ueno et al., 2018) that directly demonstrated these differences. The authors appropriately reference this established finding to provide functional context for their anatomical observations. This represents accurate attribution of prior results.

results.result: Forelimb S1 and M1 in mice are adjacent cortical areas resembling the side-by-side layout in primates, contrasting with the widely separated whisker S1 and M1 areas in mouse cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by the anatomical observations in the current study and established knowledge of cortical organization in mice and primates. The comparison is valid and helps contextualize the findings within broader mammalian neuroanatomy.

results.result: The forelimb subfield of mouse S1 shows cortical magnification of the hand relative to the rest of the forelimb, and of the thumb/thenar relative to the rest of the hand, a pattern conserved across mammalian species from rodents to primates and humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by direct anatomical observations (Figure 1) and multiple citations to studies in various mammalian species (Sur et al., 1978; Waters et al., 1995; Jain et al., 2008; Krubitzer et al., 2011; Martuzzi et al., 2014). The cortical magnification is clearly visible in the anatomical data and the conservation across species is well-documented.

results.result: PRV tracing experiments did not reveal evidence for a cuneo-PO paralemniscal pathway in mice (unlike the trigemino-PO pathway in whisker circuits), and muscle injections labeled only M1 corticospinal neurons, not S1.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by direct observations from PRV tracing experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C). The negative results are important for establishing differences between hand and whisker circuits. The muscle injection result is consistent with prior work (Ueno et al., 2018). However, negative results should be interpreted cautiously as they may reflect technical limitations rather than absence of connections.

results.result: Feedforward thalamocortical circuits largely avoid direct innervation of thalamus-projecting neurons and instead engage intratelencephalic neurons, with PO inputs showing particularly strong bias toward L5A neurons that participate in multiple circuit types.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 represent a synthesis of the connectivity patterns observed throughout the study. The conclusion is supported by the systematic characterization of inputs to different neuron types (Figures 4-5). The interpretation about circuit organization is reasonable, though it represents an inference from the data rather than a direct demonstration.

results.result: The transcortical circuit can be conceptualized as an extended set of intersecting and selectively interconnecting looping circuits, within which feedforward circuits are fully embedded.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 represents a conceptual interpretation of the circuit architecture. While this conceptualization is consistent with the findings, it is speculative and not directly tested. The claim is marked as INFERENCE and SPECULATION in the evidence type, indicating it goes beyond what is directly demonstrated.

results.result: Hand-related circuits generally resemble whisker-related circuits in excitatory connection patterns for both lemniscal and paralemniscal pathways, including the pattern of corticocortical projections targeting upper-layer neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by systematic comparison to extensive prior work on whisker circuits (multiple citations). The similarity in connectivity patterns is well-documented. The comparison to whisker S1-to-M1 projections (Mao et al., 2011) is appropriate and strengthens the conclusion about conserved organizational features.

results.result: The polysynaptic cortical organization suggests multiple possibilities for regulatory mechanisms and may increase computational power by providing diverse targets for modulatory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are speculative interpretations of the functional implications of the circuit architecture. While these are reasonable hypotheses, they are not directly tested in the study. The claims are marked as INFERENCE and SPECULATION, indicating they represent potential future directions rather than established findings.

results.result: Mice are a favorable model for investigating hand-related transcortical circuits, displaying diverse forelimb movements and having well-defined hand/forelimb representations in S1 and corticospinal projections to cervical spinal circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 are supported by multiple citations to studies of mouse forelimb behavior and anatomy (Whishaw et al., 1998; Guo et al., 2015; Galiñanes et al., 2018; Barrett et al., 2020; Ueno et al., 2018). The characterization of mice as a suitable model is well-justified and provides important context for the study.

results.result: While the macroscopic structure of hand-related transcortical pathways is well-known from classical anatomy, the cellular-level synaptic connectivity remains largely uncharacterized, contrasting with the well-studied whisker-barrel system.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 accurately characterize the state of knowledge in the field, supported by appropriate citations to classical work (Brodal, 1981; Andersson, 1995) and reviews of whisker circuits (Feldmeyer, 2012; Feldmeyer et al., 2013; Petersen, 2019; Staiger and Petersen, 2021). This establishes the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

results.result: Whisker and hand/forelimb systems differ fundamentally in sensor structure, proprioceptive systems, modes of operation, and anatomical organization, with differences potentially reflecting behavioral specializations including a more prominent role of somatosensory feedback in forelimb control.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by established knowledge and appropriate citations (Moore et al., 2015; Severson et al., 2019; Colechio and Alloway, 2009). The differences are well-documented and the inference about functional implications is reasonable, though speculative. This provides important context for comparing the two systems.
